## LiRTest: Augmenting LiDAR Point Clouds for Automated Testing of Autonomous Driving Systems

An Guo

guoan218@smail.nju.edu.cn State Key Laboratory for Novel Software Technology Nanjing University Nanjing 210023, China

## ABSTRACT

Withthe tremendous advancement of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), autonomous driving systems (ADS) have achieved significant development and been applied to assist in many safety-critical tasks. However, despite their spectacular progress, several real-world accidents involving autonomous cars even resulted in a fatality. While the high complexity and low interpretability of DNN models, which empowers the perception capability of ADS, make conventional testing techniques inapplicable for the perception of ADS, the existing testing techniques depending on manual data collection and labeling become time-consuming and prohibitively expensive.

In this paper, we design and implement LiRTest, the first automated LiDAR-based autonomous vehicles testing tool. LiRTest implements the ADS-specific metamorphic relation and equips affine and weather transformation operators that can reflect the impact of the various environmental factors to implement the relation. Weexperiment LiRTest with multiple 3D object detection models to evaluate its performance on different tasks. The experiment results show that LiRTest can activate different neurons of the object detection models and effectively detect their erroneous behaviors under various driving conditions. Also, the results confirm that LiRTest can improve the object detection precision by retraining with the generated data.

## 1 INTRODUCTION

The development of autonomous vehicles has achieved tremendous achievement over the past decade with the rapid improvement of artificial intelligence and sensor technology [26, 56]. As a typical safety-critical intelligent software, autonomous driving systems use sensors such as light detection and ranging (LiDAR) and camera to capture surrounding environment information as input and automatically complete different driving tasks by various functional components. Several major car manufacturers and organizations, including Tesla, Waymo/Google, Uber, and Baidu, are building and actively testing these cars. Recent results demonstrate that autonomous vehicles have become very efficient in practice and have already driven millions of miles without any human intervention [4].

However, such intelligent systems often demonstrate incorrect and unexpected corner case behaviors that can lead to a fatal collision when deployed in real-world environments. Various such real-world cases have already been reported [1, 2]. For instance, Tesla's self-driving vehicle rammed the truck directly in 2019 [3], the crash resulted from a failure to distinguish a white truck from a bright sky, and the radar failed because the truck was too high. Since these cars complete driving tasks based on their environment as measured by different sensors (e.g., camera, LiDAR, etc.), the space of possible inputs is extremely large, leading to numerous corner cases. There is an urgent need to explore a better approach to effectively testing self-driving software.

Recent testing techniques [47, 57, 59] demonstrate autonomous driving systems are not robust to synthetic images of driving scenes. DeepTest [47] designs systematic ways to automatically generate test cases, which methodology is to transform labeled images of driving scenes by applying various effect filters such as fog/rain and simple affine transformations to the original images and check if the systems perform consistently among the original and transformed scenes. DeepRoad [57] proposes an unsupervised DNN-based framework for automatically testing the DNN-based autonomous driving systems. It can produce more realistic driving scenes with various weather conditions by applying Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) along with the corresponding real-world weather scenes. Moreover, DeepBillBoard [59], a systematic physical-world testing approach, focuses on generating a sufficiently robust and resilient printable physical-world adversarial billboard test.

Although these approaches mentioned above have successfully found various erroneous behaviors in autonomous driving systems, there is little attention on studying the impact of point clouds collected by LiDAR under adverse environmental conditions. LiDAR is one of the most critical sensors in autonomous driving systems, which perceives the surrounding environment through distance measurements by transmitting lasers and processing laser returns [14]. Besides, it provides highly accurate range measurements that enable reliable detection performance [11, 30]. Moreover, unlike the camera, it is not affected by light, which can function well at night. However, these sensors are well known to be sensitive to adverse conditions [5, 21, 24, 41]. Based on the above reasons, it is crucial to design an automated testing approach of LiDAR-based autonomous driving software.

First, in the operating environment of the autonomous driving system, the point clouds sensed by LiDAR may be affected by various environmental factors, including adverse weather (e.g., fog, rain, snow, etc.). These effects may cause varying degrees of attenuation of the perceived point clouds or various types of noise information, which may cause erroneous behaviors in the operation of the autonomous driving system. Next, the testing process of modern autonomous driving systems heavily depends on the collected dataset, and point clouds are usually collected by LiDAR in real-road testing. Because of the diverse environmental conditions, it requires many resource consumptions to collect point clouds under different environmental factors. Finally, the manual labeling for point clouds is a laborious and time-consuming task that needs a massive workforce to manually examine the visualization results of the point clouds.

To address these issues, in this paper, we design and implement a systematic LiDAR-based automated testing tool, namely LiRTest, for automatically testing object detection systems of self-driving cars and further retrain to improve them. LiRTest can generate testing point clouds from the seed testing data, i.e., labeled point clouds, with transformation operators. Moreover, LiRTest employs transformation-specific metamorphic relations between the transformed point clouds and seed data to detect the faults automatically.

We conduct experiments with four state-of-the-art 3D object detection models to evaluate LiRTest. First, we leverage the notion of neuron coverage to explore the similarity of neurons activated by different realistic transformations in the 3D object detection model. Next, we demonstrate that average precision (AP) has decreased significantly after applying transformation operators. Further, the experimental results show that the generated data can substantially increase the AP of models after retraining. The results indicate that LiRTest can detect many erroneous behaviors and improve the robustness of the autonomous driving system by retraining the model with transformed data.

The primary contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows:

- We design two families of operators that simulate the realistic impacts of usage scenarios of LiDAR-based autonomous driving software systems. Specifically, we develop a physicsbased model to simulate LiDAR point clouds for different weather conditions.
- We implement the proposed techniques into an automated testing tool LiRTest. To the best of our knowledge, LiRTest is the first systematic and automated testing tool for LiDARbased autonomous vehicles. We have made the source code of LiRTest available 1 and released the generated transformed point clouds.
- We employ LiRTest to test four typical DNN models for 3D object detection and found various inconsistent detection results, many of which may cause potentially fatal collisions. The results show that the synthetic point clouds can be used for retraining and making object detection systems more robust to different corner cases.

## 2 AUTONOMOUS DRIVING SYSTEMS

## 2.1 The Architecture of Autonomous Driving Systems

Autonomous driving technologies vary in the ability of automation. The Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) proposes six levels of vehicle autonomy [42], with Level 0 (L0) being the lowest, and Level 5 (L5) being the highest. In this section, we focus on L4 autonomous driving systems since they have the highest autonomy level among the autonomous driving systems in production today. Their software bugs and defects are extremely important in terms of safety and robustness for this reason. Fig.1 shows the general modular-based autonomous driving software system architecture based on state-of-the-art designs. As shown, such a software system is responsible for all the core decision-making steps after receiving sensor input. The detailed functionality of each component in an autonomous driving software system is as follows:

Sensors first perceive surrounding environment at set intervals, running scenarios are constructed and put into the perception module. Perception is in charge of collecting and processing environmental information and in-vehicle information via various sensors to achieve the functionalities such as object detection, path selection, lane detection, and scene reconstruction. This component is responsible for detecting obstacles such as vehicles and pedestrians. Autonomous driving systems often adopt multiple object detection pipelines to avoid false detection. For example, Baidu Apollo is made up of a LiDAR-based and a camera-based object detection pipeline, which uses segmentation models based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). And then data fusion algorithms such as a Kalman filter process the detected obstacles from different pipelines. After receiving the processed information, the decision and planning module estimates the future trajectory of the detected obstacles in time and space dimensions and calculates the optimal driving trajectory considering various factors such as safety and speed. Next, the vehicle control module calculates and executes the planned trajectory with lateral and longitudinal control. Finally, CAN is in charge of sending control commands and receiving chassis information.

The object detection tasks lay the foundation of the perception module and autonomous driving systems' workflow and significantly impact the final behaviors [19]. In this paper, we employ LiDAR-based 3D object detection task to evaluate the performance of LiRTest.

## 2.2 3D Object Detection with LiDAR Point Clouds

In the context of autonomous driving, LiDAR refers to a broad category of sensors that use reflected light to measure the geometry of the surrounding environment near the vehicle. The most commonly used type of LiDAR sensor in autonomous driving is the time-of-flight (TOF) systems [32], which obtain distance and reflect intensity information of objects to be measured. LiDAR sensors are widely employed in 3D object detection for capturing 3D scene information as irregular and sparse point clouds, which provide crucial cues for 3D scene perception and understanding.

3D object detection has been drawing increasing attention from both industry and academia thanks to its wide applications in autonomous driving. Given single or multi-sensor data as input, the target of the 3D object detection task is to classify and localize objects in 3D space. Object detection with LiDAR point clouds is an intrinsically three-dimensional problem. According to point cloud representations, most existing 3D detection methods could be classified into two categories, i.e., the grid-based methods and the point-based methods. To tackle the irregular data format problem of point clouds, the grid-based methods generally project the irregular point clouds to regular representations such as 3D voxels [12, 60] or 2D bird-view maps [29, 54], which could be efficiently processed by 2D or 3D CNNs. Instead, PointNet and its variants [39, 40], the point-based methods [35, 44, 55] directly extract features from raw point clouds for 3D detection. Point-based methods manifest strong capabilities and great potential in the 3D detection task.

In general, the grid-based methods are more computationally efficient, but the unavoidable information loss reduces the finegrained localization accuracy, while the point-based methods have higher computation cost but could achieve a larger receptive field by the point set abstraction with ease [40]. Then a novel 3D object detection framework PV-RCNN [43] is proposed to integrate the best of the two types of methods, and significantly surpass the prior state-of-the-art 3D detection methods.

In spite of the promising detection performance in the normal situation, it is challenging to promote 3D object detection in commercial applications [49]. First, It is hard to extract features of objects with few points due to sparsely distributed scan points in 3D space. Next, rain and fog particles are easily reflected by LiDAR and lead to noise points in the natural outdoor scene. Therefore, researchers should develop a robust object detection algorithm to handle noisy input. Besides, detection performance relies much on the training dataset containing diverse scenarios, and developers cannot calibrate network parameters for different application conditions easily. Finally, the efficiency of exploring irregular points and whether to fuse multi-sensor data are other two challenging issues.

## 3 APPROACH

LiRTest is a systematic and automatic tool for testing LiDAR-based autonomous vehicles. As shown in Fig.2, domain experts design physical and geometric models to simulate the properties of LiDAR under different adverse weather conditions and a linear mapping between two point clouds, respectively. Then the transformation operators (e.g., RN, TR etc.) are defined according to the model construction. Next, the developer selects point cloud seeds from real-world data, leverages the point cloud processing unit to identify and process them, and implements the mutation algorithm based on transformation operators. After that, the transformed test data can be generated to evaluate the robustness of the 3D object detection model of autonomous driving. Finally, we get test reports based on detection bounding boxes and give feedback on operator design. Besides, LiRTest can improve the model's AP by retraining with the transformed training data.

## 3.1 Metamorphic Testing for Autonomous Driving Object Detection System

Amajor challenge in testing the complex LiDAR-based autonomous vehicle system is to create the system's specifications manually. Besides, the annotation of the 3D point clouds consumes a large amount of time. To avoid these issues, we leverage metamorphic relations (MRs) [8, 9] between the car detection results across the original point cloud and its transformed point cloud. The core idea is that we can define relationships between the model detection results across certain types of transformations. The violation of MRs often indicates potential defects.

LiRTest is designed to realize the affine and weather MRs for LiDAR-based autonomous driving systems. Specifically, we denote the object detection systems of autonomous driving as OD that detects the car, pedestrian and cyclists, etc. The MRs can be defined as given a seed point cloud C , and transformations operators 𝛾 ∈ T can generate various point clouds from each point cloud 𝑐 ∈ C . The affine MR to test OD with additional transformed point clouds adopted in this research can be formalized as follows:

where 𝜁 is a criterion asserting the equality of OD results. The given affine MR is defined such that object detection results of the transformed point cloud are expected to agree with those applying the affine operator 𝛾 on the original results. Similar to affine transformation, the weather MR to test OD with additional transformed point clouds can be formalized as follows:

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

The given weather MR is defined such that no matter how the point cloud is synthesized by applying weather transformation operators 𝛾 on c, the object detection results are expected to be consistent with those in the original point cloud. Thus, if an OD infers a set of 3D bounding boxes 𝐵 0 for an input seed point cloud 𝑐 and a set of 3D bounding boxes 𝐵 𝑡 for a newly transformed point cloud 𝑐 𝑡 , which is generated by applying the weather transformation 𝛾 on 𝑐 . 𝐵 0 and 𝐵 𝑡 should be identical, otherwise erroneous predictions can be revealed by checking the failure of this MR. Note that the only difference between weather and affine MRs lies in that the affine transformations require applying the corresponding operators 𝛾 to obtain the correct labels for the augmented data, while weather transformations preserve the same labels before and after the transformation process.

However, asserting the equality of OD outputs is too strict; there is usually no single correct detection result for a given point cloud, which may result in a large number of false positives. In order to make the MRs more permissive, our equality criteria 𝜁 is derived from Average Precision (AP) [15]. The AP score is calculated by taking both 'precision' and 'recall' values into account, as we explain in Section 4.3.

Given affine and weather MRs, we can simply check the test oracle whether it is satisfied in the testing process of OD . Under this setting, the design and implementation of transformation operators come to be crucial for the performance of LiRTest.

## 3.2 Transformation Operators

In this section, we clarify how we generate realistic augmentation inputs by applying transformation operators on seed point clouds and mimic different real-world phenomena like object movements, different weather conditions, etc.

To this end, we investigate seven different realistic point cloud transformation operators: translation (TR), rotation (RO), scale (SC), symmetry (SY), rain (RN), snow (SW), and fog (FG). These transformations can be classified into two categories: affine and weather. We implement several transformation operators for each category and integrate them into LiRTest. The detailed definition and design are as follows:

3.2.1 Affine Transformation. An affine transformation is a linear mapping between two point clouds that preserves points, straight lines, and planes [33]. Affine transformations are often used in point cloud processing to eliminate the systematic errors resulting from the laser scanner. In this paper, we design four different types of affine transformation operators, including TR, RO, SC, and SY, and leverage them for the inverse case, i.e., to simulate different real-world LiDAR perspectives or movements of objects and check how robust the 3D object detection models are to those changes. The specific operators are as follows:

- TR translates every point 𝑝 ( 𝑥,𝑦, 𝑧 ) such that a transformed point 𝑝 ∗ has the form 𝑝 ( 𝑥 + 𝑡 𝑥 , 𝑦 + 𝑡 𝑦 , 𝑧 + 𝑡 𝑧 ) . The parameters of TR are 𝑡 𝑥 , 𝑡 𝑦 and 𝑡 𝑧 , which mean the amount of translation along the x, y, z-axis, respectively.
- RO rotates every point 𝑝 ( 𝑥,𝑦, 𝑧 ) around the upright 𝑧 axis by an angle 𝑞 .
- SC scales every point 𝑝 ( 𝑥,𝑦, 𝑧 ) in every direction by a scalar such that a transformed point 𝑝 ∗ has the form 𝑝 ( 𝑠 𝑥 ∗ 𝑥, 𝑠 𝑦 ∗ 𝑦, 𝑠 𝑧 ∗ 𝑧 ) .
- SY manipulates every point 𝑝 ( 𝑥,𝑦, 𝑧 ) such that a transformed point 𝑝 ∗ has the form 𝑝 ( 𝑥, -𝑦, 𝑧 ) . Note that in order to ensure the realness of the generated data, we make all points symmetrical about the 𝑋𝑂𝑍 plane.

RN Specific Characteristics. Rain may have another two impacts on LiDAR. First, the number of detected points decreases due to scattering from rain droplets [21]. Secondly, the presence of rain also introduces noise to the range measurement [41]. ## 4 EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN

In this section, we introduce our experimental setup, including the dataset and 3D object detection models under-tested, approaches of affine and weather transformations, evaluation metrics, and the research questions we study in the experiments. To conduct the experiments, we implement the augmentation approach upon PCL 1.8.1 2 on Windows 10 operating system. And the evaluation parts are performed on a Ubuntu 18.04.3 LTS server with 8 Tesla V100SXM2 GPUs, one 10-core processor with 2.50GHz and 32GB physical memory.

LiRTest is designed to systematically test the LiDAR-based autonomous driving system, especially to verify its robustness for the 3D object detection module. To this end, we empirically explore the following three research questions (RQ):

- RQ1: Do different realistic point clouds transformations activate different neurons?
- RQ2: How effective are different transformation methods for detecting the erroneous behaviors of 3D object detection task using MRs?

2 https://pointclouds.org/

- RQ3: Can we retrain the 3D detection model with synthetic point clouds to improve AP?

## 4.1 Dataset and 3D Object Detection Models

KITTI (Karlsruhe Institute of Technology and Toyota Technological Institute) [20] is one of the most popular datasets in the autonomous driving research field. The dataset consists of hours of driving data collected by various sensors (laser scanners, grayscale cameras, color cameras, etc.) in real driving scenarios. Specifically, KITTI adopts a Velodyne HDL-64E rotating 3D laser scanner as a sensor setup. Each collected point is stored with its ( 𝑥,𝑦, 𝑧 ) coordinate and an additional reflectance value ( 𝑟 ) . The KITTI dataset only partially provides the ground-truth information; meanwhile, prior researchers have also manually labeled parts. The 3D object detection benchmarks, where the dataset is most widely used, contain 3712 training images, 3769 validation images, and 7518 test images, and the corresponding point clouds, which consist of 80,256 labeled objects. In this paper, we discuss the train/validation split of the point clouds set because a separate test set is available for KITTI, whose labels are not disclosed.

LiDAR-based 3D Object Detection Models. To evaluate the performance of our techniques effectively, we choose four state-ofthe-art models as the testing subjects in the experiment. We briefly introduce them as follows:

PointPillars model [29] is a novel encoder that leverages PointNets [39] to learn point clouds representations organized in vertical columns. It outperforms previous encoders with regard to both speed and accuracy by a large margin. It is widely used in the opensource autonomous driving systems Apollo 3 and Autoware 4 .

SECOND model [53] investigates an improved sparse convolution method for voxel-based 3D convolutional networks, significantly increasing training and inference speed. The detector consists of three components: a voxelwise feature extractor, a sparse convolutional middle layer, and an RPN.

Part-A 2 model [45] extends the preliminary work PointRCNN [44] to a part-aware and aggregation neural network. The whole framework consists of the part-aware stage and the part-aggregation stage. The former is designed to predict high-quality 3D proposals and accurate intra-object part locations, while the latter learns to re-score the box and refine the box location.

PV-RCNN model [43] integrates both 3D voxel CNN and PointNetbased set abstraction to learn more point cloud features, which combines the advantages of efficient learning and high-quality proposals of the 3D voxel CNN and the flexible receptive fields of the PointNet-based networks.

To verify whether LiRTest is effective in testing autonomous driving systems, we select OpenPCDet 5 , which is a straightforward, simple, self-contained open source project for LiDAR-based 3D object detection to investigate the test techniques proposed in this paper empirically. The project has 2.3k stars on GitHub. We employ default parameter settings and obtain pre-trained models from the model zoo.

## 4.2 Affine and Weather Transformations

LiRTest focuses on improving the robustness of the 3D object detection model in adverse driving conditions by making realistic affine and weather transformations. As described in Section 3.2, we mainly apply seven different realistic point cloud transformation operators: i.e. TR, RO, SC, SY, RN, SW, and FG. In order to make our transformations realistic, we control the translation distance, rotation angle, and scaling amount for affine transformations and generate LiDAR point clouds with different rainfall, snowfall, and fog concentration. In our experiment design, hyperparameters 𝜎 and 𝑅 are set as 8 and 1.35, candidate parameters for each transformation are shown in Table 2. Note that the symmetry operator has no parameters. Whenever the transformation operator is applied to original data, we randomly select the parameters for a specific transformation.

## 4.3 Evaluation Metric

The main task of a 3D object detection model is to predict the 3D bounding box's coordinates around an object when it is present in an input point cloud. The central concept for evaluating the 3D object detection task is Intersection over Union (IoU), which compares the coordinates of ground truth and predicted 3D bounding boxes [36]. And we express it as follows:

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

Formally, IoU measures the overlap (intersection) area between a ground-truth 3D bounding box 𝐵 𝑔𝑡 and a predicted 3D bounding box 𝐵 𝑝 over their union. In our experiments evaluation, for cars, we require a 3D bounding box overlap of 70%, while for pedestrians and cyclists, we require a 3D bounding box overlap of 50%.

Then we employ the AP to measure the testing performance of LiRTest and answer research questions. To achieve a more fair comparison of the results, we follow the suggestions of the Mapillary team in their paper [46] and use 40 recall positions instead of the 11 recall positions proposed in the original Pascal VOC benchmark [15], which is defined as follows:

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

We apply exactly forty equally spaced recall levels, i.e. 𝑅 40 = { 1 / 40 , 2 / 40 , 3 / 40 , . . . , 1 } . The interpolation function is defined as 𝜌 interp ( 𝑟 ) = max 𝑟 ′ : 𝑟 ′ ≥ 𝑟 𝜌 ( 𝑟 ′ ) , where 𝜌 ( 𝑟 ) gives the precision at recall 𝑟 .

## 5 RESULT ANALYSIS AND DISCUSSION

## 5.1 Answer to RQ1

In order to explore whether synthetic point clouds generated by applying different realistic point cloud transformations can activate different neurons. We randomly pick 300 input point clouds from the test set and transform each of them by using seven different transformation operators: RN, SW, FG, TR, RO, SC, SY. We also randomly select the parameters of each transformation and generate a total of 2100 new synthetic point clouds. We run all models with these seed and synthetic point clouds as input and then record the neurons activated by each input. We apply the neuron coverage metrics proposed in DeepXplore [37] to calculate the neuron coverage and use 0.5 as the neuron activation threshold for our experiments.

We then compare the neurons activated by different synthetic point clouds generated from the same point clouds. Let us assume that two transformations 𝑇 1 and 𝑇 2, when applied to an original point cloud 𝑐 , activate two sets of neurons 𝑆 1 and 𝑆 2 respectively. We measure the dissimilarities between 𝑆 1 and 𝑆 2 by measuring their Jaccard distance: 1 - | 𝑆 1 ∩ 𝑆 2 | | 𝑆 1 ∪ 𝑆 2 | . We also compute the neuron activation sets dissimilarities between per point cloud transformation and the corresponding seed point cloud.

Results. Figure 3 presents the result for all possible pairs of point cloud seeds and transformations (e.g., Seed vs. RN, Seed vs. RO, etc.) for different models. And we also calculate the mean value of the Jaccard distance for each combines of model and operator to illustrate the neuron activation sets dissimilarities from another perspective, as shown in Table 3. For all models, the SW operator consistently has a much higher median Jaccard distance (up to 0.49) and mean Jaccard distance (up to 0.47) than other operators, which indicates a significant difference between the neuron activated by the SW and the original seed. Besides, the minimum median Jaccard distance for each model, from left to right, is 0.09, 0.07, 0.11, and 0.14.

Figure 4 shows the result for all possible pair of transformations (e.g., RN vs. SW, SW vs. SC, etc.) for different models. As shown in the figure, the median Jaccard distance for PointPillars , SECOND , Part-A 2 and PV-RCNN models are 0.35, 0.28, 0.22, and 0.32. And the mean Jaccard distances for the four tested models are 0.36, 0.29, 0.24, and 0.31. In addition, the interquartile range for PointPillars , SECOND , Part-A 2 , and PV-RCNN models is 0.24 ∼ 0.48, 0.18 ∼ 0.39, 0.16 ∼ 0.29, and 0.25 ∼ 0.37.

Figure 5: Testing results on different models with seven transformation operators.

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Discussion. Figure 3 and Table 3 explore the activation difference between the original point cloud and the transformed point cloud. We found the transformed data triggered different DNNs internal logic in the 3D object detection model relative to the seed data. Additionally, we speculate that the SW operator has the highest median and mean Jaccard distance because it imposes noise on the seed data. Figure 4 demonstrates high neuron activation sets dissimilarities; that is, different point cloud transformations activate different sets of neurons. Some existing studies have confirmed that neuron coverage is a good metric to capture the input-output diversity of DNNs; hence our experimental results indicate each transformation operator has unique characteristics and increase the diversity of the inputs.

## 5.2 Answer to RQ2

To verify whether the augmentation test point clouds can efficiently and effectively detect the erroneous behaviors, LiRTest applies seven transformations introduced in Section 3.2 for each tested model on the original test set 𝑇 𝑂 to generate test point clouds. To avoid the inconsistency between the size of the augmentation test dataset 𝑇 𝐴 and the original test dataset 𝑇 𝑂 , LiRTest generates the same size of transformed datasets as 𝑇 𝑂 for each transformation operator. Then the transformed dataset 𝑇 𝐴 = { 𝑇 𝑅𝑁 , 𝑇 𝑆𝑊 , 𝑇 𝐹𝐺 , 𝑇 𝑇𝑅 , 𝑇 𝑅𝑂 𝑇 𝑆𝐶 , 𝑇 𝑆𝑌 } are put into the pre-trained model 𝑀 to make the model predict and calculate the AP of car, pedestrian, and cyclist, respectively. Note that the average accuracy of most models on the original test set is relatively high. For the test set generated by our tool, the drop of AP indicates that LiRTest can effectively detect the potential defects of the tested model.

Results. Fig.5 presents the moderately difficulty results of RQ2, which show the AP difference of car, pedestrian, and cyclist of all models for the test set 𝑇 𝑂 and 𝑇 𝐴 . The AP performance decrease of the car for all models is 7.59%, the pedestrian is 11.41%, and the cyclist is 14.27%. Moreover, the accuracy on transformed test sets has decreased more significantly for weather transformation than affine transformation. Table 4 further elaborates the mean average precision (mAP) on the moderate level for 𝑇 𝑂 and 𝑇 𝐴 . Then we find that mAP of each configuration decrease by a different degree. PointPillars , SECOND , Part-A 2 , and PV-RCNN models drop by up to 44.53% (SW), 18.45% (RN), 26.06% (RN), 26.80% (RN) for all transformations, respectively. Obviously, our approach can find defects for all detection models, despite the different performance of each model.

To prove the effectiveness of LiRTest in detecting erroneous behaviors, we intercepted some errors found by LiRTest, as shown in Fig. 6. For each transformation method, we list two group real examples of erroneous predictions in the tested model. As shown in the figure, the first two rows and the last two rows are the errors (marked with red lines) detected by applying weather and affine transformation when the original data are pedestrian and vehicle, respectively. There are two main types of errors; one is the model predicts the wrong 3D detection bounding box (marked with red cuboid), and the other is the model cannot detect the ground truth object (marked with the red circle). Although only a little modification is added to the original point cloud, the detection objects predicted by the model is completely changed.

Discussion. After analysis, we discover that adverse weather plays a critical role in affecting LiDAR detection performance and models are more prone to erroneous behaviors for weather transformations than affine transformation. For example, the object detection module of PointPillars strikes in snowy days. And model detection performance drops significantly in rainy and snowy adverse conditions, according to Table 4. Indeed, the autonomous driving system does not work properly in severe rain or snow, as mentioned in the above sections. Besides, model performance will be improved under certain circumstances (e.g., the second model detects pedestrians after applying the SC operator). Additionally, most models are more robust to detecting cars than pedestrians and cyclists after applying weather transformations, thus car detection may be less susceptible to noise disturbance. Last but not least, we can't interpret the model running logic and root cause of the faults, though presenting erroneous predictions in Fig. 6. We leave it as interesting future work.

## 5.3 Answer to RQ3

Here we check whether retraining the 3D object detection models with some of the synthetic point clouds generated by LiRTest helps in making the models more robust. LiRTest applies seven transformations on the original training set 𝑅 𝑂 and generates the exact size of transformed datasets as 𝑅 𝑂 for each transformation operator. Then we mix the transformed dataset 𝑅 𝐴 = { 𝑅 𝑅𝑁 , 𝑅 𝑆𝑊 , 𝑅 𝐹𝐺 , 𝑅 𝑇𝑅 , 𝑅 𝑅𝑂 , 𝑅 𝑆𝐶 , 𝑅 𝑆𝑌 } . In order to reduce the retraining time cost for the pre-trained model, we randomly select a small amount of data from mixed transformed point clouds to train for all configurations. We leverage the transformed testing data to answer RQ3. Specifically, we employ the affine and weather transformation methods of LiRTest to generate a transformed test set with the same size as the original test set.

Results. Table 5 presents the AP of all models at different levels of difficulty after retraining with the transformed data generated by LiRTest. We keep the experimental configuration of retraining consistent with the initial training model process, and the retraining epoch is set as 40. The test result shown in the table is that we selected 10% size of the mixed transformed data along with the original training data for retraining. The promotion range of PointPillars , SECOND , Part-A 2 and PV-RCNN is 4.22% ∼ 11.67%, 0.31% ∼ 3.98%, 2.99% ∼ 8.55% and 1.41% ∼ 15.43%, respectively. We further compute the performance improvement of mAP on the moderate level for each model; the calculated results for PointPillars , SECOND , Part-A 2 , and PV-RCNN are 6.27%, 3.09%, 6.14%, and 7.06%. By category, the cyclist has the most average retraining performance improvement, reaching 8.4%, and the car has the least, only 4.06%. Our experiments show that using transformed data generated by LiRTest for retraining can significantly improve the AP of the model on the 3D object detection task.

Discussion. Table 5 demonstrates that the quality of the retraining data is relatively high. If the size of the retraining data set is too large, it will consume a lot of resources during the training process. In contrast, in our experiments, a small number of point clouds used for retraining may effectively improve the performance of the model. From the experimental results, we found that the degree of improvement is correlated with the original detection precision. For instance, tested on the transformed test set, the pre-trained model has good performance on car detection (&gt; 65% or even &gt; 70% based on the moderately difficult results) than others. Thus relatively high AP may limit the room for model improvement.

## 5.4 Threats to Validity

Data Selection. Data selection is one of the primary threats to validity. We only employ the KITTI dataset to validate LiRTest. While we adopt a variety of transformation operators, the limitation of the experiment dataset may threaten the generality of the results. The original dataset can fundamentally affect the quality of the transformed data. Therefore, for input point clouds with driving scenes that do not exist in the training set (e.g., dust), the retrained model may not predict correctly. However, KITTI is one of the most widely-used datasets in the research community on autonomous driving systems [20]. It is collected from diverse driving scenes, which shows that the experiment results could be generalized to other datasets.

Impacts of Other Factors. One threat to validity comes from the data simulation. There are many other factors (e.g., electromagnetic waves) that may mutate the reflected point clouds and thus influence the behaviors of autonomous driving systems. These potential impacts may threaten the application of our technique. However, while this paper makes the first attempt to design the realistic mutations of the point cloud, it cannot cover all factors that may influence the performance of LiDAR. We plan to explore the impact of other factors in future research.

Data Simulation. In this paper, we design the seven transformation operators to simulate environmental impacts on the LiDAR sensors. Even though our transformations are designed based on several existing research on LiDAR sensors, the generated point clouds may not be exactly the same in the real world due to various unpredictable factors, such as the back-scattering coefficient of the target, the parameters of the LiDAR sensors and so on. To alleviate this threat, we plan to further fine-tune the parameter of the proposed operators based on more empirical studies and data collected from realistic scenes.

Parameter Settings. Another threat could be caused by the configurable transformation parameters. Some of our results might not generalize to other parameters in the evaluation. To alleviate this threat, we use a large number of parameters that match the real driving environment in our experiment design; candidate parameters for each transformation are discussed in Section 4.2.

The Testing Functionality Selection. LiDAR-based object detection is just one of the subtasks for driving an autonomous vehicle; follow-up tasks, including object tracking and sensor fusion, etc., also affect the final decision of the autonomous driving system. Even though the experimental results suggest that transformed point clouds are effective in detecting the incorrect perception predictions and improving the AP of 3D object detection tasks, it is hard to guarantee the effectiveness of LiRTest in improving safety for the whole driving system.

## 6 RELATED WORK

In this section, we primarily introduce the related works on two aspects: testing approaches of autonomous driving systems and metamorphic testing.

## 6.1 Testing and Verification of DNN-Driven Autonomous Driving Systems

Automatically generating and constructing diverse and challenging driving scenes is a great challenge to test DNN-based autonomous driving systems due to the sheer number and the complexity of possible traffic scenarios [23, 58]. A recent set of approaches [31, 47, 57] leverage differential and metamorphic testing techniques for identifying inputs that trigger inconsistencies among different DNN models, or among the original and transformed driving scenes. Moreover, DeepBillBoard [59], a systematic physical-world testing approach, is capable of generating a robust and resilient adversarial test and misleading the behaviors of the neural networks by inserting special marks on the roadside billboards. Gambi Alessio et al. [18] combine search-based testing and procedural content generation to generate effective test suites and expose many safetycritical failures related to lane-keeping in multiple configurations. Daniel J. Fremont et al. [17] developed a probabilistic programming language called SCENIC, which can help to generate specialized driving scenes for analysis and testing perception systems.

The key differences between the related work mentioned above and LiRTest are threefold: (1) These related studies focus on mutating images to find various erroneous behaviors, while our testing and enhancement approach designs affine and weather transformation operators and generates transformed test point clouds from original point clouds collected by LiDAR, which plays an important role in autonomous driving; (2) The transformation approach in LiRTest for generating test samples aims to test the perception module for the modular-based autonomous driving software system (Apollo, Autoware, etc.). In contrast, the data generated in other related works verify the end-to-end self-driving cars, and (3) A physics-based model is proposed in LiRTest to generate massive labeled data under different weather conditions and further retrain and improve the object detection systems, while the aforementioned approaches don't adopt physical modeling to describe weather characteristics.

## 6.2 Metamorphic Testing

Metamorphic testing (MT) [8, 9] is a software testing technique used to alleviate the test oracle problem. It identifies software bugs by detecting violations of domain-specific MRs that are defined across outputs from multiple executions of the program with different inputs. Generally speaking, when conducting MT, the testers first identify an MR of the software under test and then select a test case selection strategy to generate test cases and finally check test results. In traditional software testing, researchers propose the innovative application of metamorphic testing to proving [10], debugging [28], fault localization [51], program repair [27], program slicing [52], etc.

With the rapid development of machine learning, metamorphic testing has been applied for testing classification and regression tasks [34, 48, 50, 61]. Xie et al. [50] present an MT technique for testing the machine learning classification algorithms which can detect real faults in a well-known open-source classification program. Besides, Wang et al. [48] adopts MT as an adaptive and effective testing strategy by asserting the equivalence of object detection results between the original and synthetic images to reveal defects in object detection systems. Zhou et al. [61] employ metamorphic testing in combination with fuzzing technique to detect unknown fatal errors in the LiDAR obstacle perception system of the Baidu Apollo self-driving software.

In this paper, LiRTest develops a specific LiDAR-oriented metamorphic testing module for DNN-based autonomous driving systems, where the affine and weather MRs are defined in Section 3.1. Each MR depicts the necessary properties of the target autonomous driving software in terms of inputs and their expected detection results. Consequently, erroneous predictions can be revealed by checking the failure of these MRs.

## 7 CONCLUSION

In this paper, we proposed and evaluated LiRTest, the first systematic and automated module testing tool for LiDAR-based autonomous vehicle. To enhance the abundance of test samples and discover more corner cases for the tested models, LiRTest innovatively designed seven transformation operators and generated synthetic test point clouds by applying affine and weather realistic transformations on a set of seed point clouds. We use autonomous driving domain-specific MRs to find erroneous behaviors of the 3D object detection models without detailed specifications.

LiRTest has been evaluated on four state-of-art 3D object detection models. The experiment results show that the transformed point clouds generated by LiRTest can detect erroneous behaviors efficiently and improve object detection module robustness through retraining. We believe LiRTest is a critical step towards assuring the quality of LiDAR-based autonomous driving systems.
